- By day Nell packs the kitchen. That night the things she threw out are rubbed out of the harbor.
- Oddment joins, busy mending a lighthouse that does not need mending.
- Puzzle: raise and lower the soap-dish ferry with hot and cold taps and the plug.
- Boss: the Drain, a courteous whirlpool that "only takes small things first: keys, names, the word for kettle". Nell Finishes it by Naming three swallowed words found in the map.
- First sighting of the Tidy, who leaves a thank-you note: "Pardon the mess. Nearly done."

**Chapter 3, the Staircase and the Landing of Framed Faces (Wednesday, 14 min).**
- The party climbs one step per year, past height marks that stop at "Nell, 9".
- Puzzle: match names to smudged portraits using Underdrawing rubbings.
- Comic relief comes from Coil, a tape-measure snake who is sensitive about his length, and from the very friendly six-legged Half-Dog.
- Boss: the Stranger-in-the-Hall, a towering coat scribbled so hard the paper has torn, shrieking "WHO LET YOU IN".
- When it is Finished, the scribble resolves into a small girl in a yellow raincoat. The party goes silent. Blot says, "...Oh. That's you."

**Chapter 4, Attic of Unsent Things (Thursday, 14 min).**
- There is no boss. Moths and envelopes fill the attic.
- Puzzle: order Oma's unsent weekly letters by how far the handwriting has decayed. The last is only a smiling blot.
- Nell reads, "Dear Nell, today I remembered your name all day."
- Blot's edges go dotted. Set-piece chase: the page rubs out behind the party. The Tidy offers a dustpan and asks, "There. Doesn't that hurt less?"
- Choice: "Hold on" or "Let go" of Blot's hand.
  - "Hold on" with 12 or more Finished drawings: the townsfolk flood in and redraw her outline. She survives as a faint ghost-line party member who regains color over chapter 5.
  - Otherwise her battle slot stays as an empty dotted outline that takes silent turns.

**Chapter 5, the Margin and the Last Page (Friday, 16 min).**
- Nell enters the Underdrawing proper and Dill joins.
- Puzzle: walk only on the blue perspective lines toward the vanishing point.
- The kept Keepsakes open their memories. The mandatory one is the winter hallway and the lie to Dad, which Nell must say aloud. The player has to select the line "I lied."
- Final boss: the Tidy.
  - Phase 1 floods the Swatch with Blanks.
  - In phase 2 it lifts off its eraser cap to show Nell's own face, drawn neatly, with no mouth.
- A final three-way choice follows.
**Epilogue, Saturday (5 min).** Moving day. One of three endings plays, then credits over the Endpapers gallery of every drawing the player Finished.
pitch:imagery-first.emotion_mechanic:
**THE SWATCH: one shared mood for the whole page, built by mixing colors**

Feelings are not personal statuses. They are crayon strokes that both sides layer onto a single shared strip, and the mix changes the rules for everyone in the fight.

**Layout**

The battle is an open sketchbook spread.
- Enemies are drawn large on the right page.
- The party stands as small full-body doodles in a row on a ground line along the bottom of the left page. Pencil-stub gauges under each show HP and Lead.
- The Swatch is a strip of 3 scribble slots across the top of the gutter.
- Turn order is a row of ribbon bookmarks.
- Commands pop up on a sticky note beside the active character.

**Strokes**

Every colored skill pushes 1 stroke into the Swatch (some push 2). The Swatch is first-in first-out with 3 slots.

| Primary | Feeling |
|---|---|
| Blue | Longing |
| Red | Nerve |
| Yellow | Wonder |

Jab, items and Sharpen are colorless.

**Mood is the set of colors present**

| Swatch contents | Mood | Effect on both sides |
|---|---|---|
| 1-2 Blue strokes | Blue Tint | Heals and shields +25%. Speed -10%. |
| 3 Blue strokes | Deep Blue | Heals and shields +50%. Speed -20%. Everyone regains 5% max HP per round. |
| 1-2 Red strokes | Red Tint | Damage dealt +20%. Damage taken +10%. |
| 3 Red strokes | Deep Red | Damage dealt +40%. Damage taken +25%. Crit +15%. |
| 1-2 Yellow strokes | Yellow Tint | Speed +20%. Status chance +15%. |
| 3 Yellow strokes | Deep Yellow | Speed +40%. Skills cost 1 less Lead (minimum 1). |
| Blue + Yellow | Green, Tenderness | Draw actions +50% Sketch. Damage -20%. One status cured on everyone each round. |
| Red + Yellow | Orange, Glee | Crit +25%. Each crit refunds 1 Lead. Nobody can Sharpen or guard. |
| Red + Blue | Violet, Dread | Whoever has the lower HP% deals +30%. Draw actions -50%. No fleeing. |
| All three | Brown, Muddle | Skills cost +1 Lead. Accuracy -20%. Sketch gain 0. Sharpen also lifts the oldest stroke. |

**Heart Color**

Every combatant has one. When the Mood matches it you are In Your Element: +25% to everything you do and +1 Lead regen. Enemies get the same bonus, so every fight is a tug-of-war over the room's feeling.

**Pressure (0-3, per character)**
- +1 when you act In Your Element.
- +1 when you take a hit over 25% of max HP.
- At 3 your next skill is a Bold Line: x1.5 effect, and it pushes 2 strokes.
- Then your lead Snaps: Pressure resets to 0 and you get no Lead regen next turn.

**Blend Flourish**

It triggers when your stroke turns an ally's Tint into a Blend. It is free and happens at most once per round.
- Green: the party heals 15% max HP.
- Orange: a bonus hit at 60% power.
- Violet: all enemies are Shaken (accuracy -20% for 2 turns).

**Lead (skill resource)**
- Maximum 6, rising to 10 by level 15.
- +1 per turn.
- Sharpen gives +3 Lead and halves damage taken that round.

**Erasure**
- The Tidy's forces push Blank strokes, which fill a slot with no color.
- Three Blanks make a Blank Page. All colored party skills are sealed and one buff is stripped per round.
- The only ways out are a Color-in Draw action or Dill's Lamplight.
- You beat erasure by putting feeling back on the page.
pitch:imagery-first.nonviolent_mechanic:
**FINISHING**

Enemies are unfinished or half-erased drawings. Each has HP (Ink) and a Sketch meter from 0 to 100.

**Draw actions**

| Action | Who | Cost | Base Sketch gain | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Outline | Anyone | 0 Lead | +20 | Colorless. |
| Color-in | Anyone | 1 Lead | +15 | Pushes a stroke of the color you choose. |
| Name It | Nell only | 2 Lead | +35 if the Mood equals the enemy's Missing Color, else +10 | Needs Sketch at 50 or more. |

**Modifiers**
- Outline and Color-in gains double while the Mood equals the enemy's Missing Color.
- Green adds a further +50%.
- Find the Missing Color with Blot's Peek. You can also read it from the enemy's outline, which tints toward it as you get close.
- Once an enemy is at 30% HP or below, Sketch gains are halved. A scribbled-over drawing is harder to finish, so you have to commit to one approach.

**Missing Piece**

At Sketch 50 each enemy shows a one-time bespoke action worth +30. Examples: draw the Odd Sock its twin, address the Unsent Envelope, give the Eyeless Duck eyes. For Half-Dog the right answer is to correct nothing and simply name it "Good Dog". Finishing is not fixing.

**Signing**

At 100 you Sign it. The drawing leaves happily, appears in the Endpapers gallery, and moves into Button Square as an NPC with a gift, a joke, a hint or shop stock.

**Rewards**

| Outcome | Graphite (XP) | Shavings (money) | Effect on the town |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scribbling Out (HP to 0) | 100% | Yes | A black scrawl is left on the map and the town stays emptier. |
| Finishing | 70% | None | The drawing moves in as an NPC. |

**Bosses**

Bosses are Oma's memories. A Scribbled Out boss leaves a blank page in the real book.

**Crumbs and Tidy-Ups**

They have nothing to finish and cannot be Finished. They can be swept away, which is a free flee.
endings:
**A. THE LAST PAGE**

Requirements:
- Finish at least 3 of the 4 bosses.
- Save Blot in chapter 4 (choose "Hold on" with 12 or more Finished drawings).
- Pick "Draw it together" at the final choice. The option is greyed out to a ghost line unless the other two conditions are met.

What happens:
- Nell tells Dad the truth about the lie, and he hugs her in the car park.
- At the care home Oma does not know her name. She sees the blot on page 3 and laughs: "That's my best mistake."
- Two hands on one pencil, one spotted and shaky and one small and smudged, draw the lamplight on the last page. The leitmotif finally resolves to its home note.
- A caption reads: "She forgot again by teatime. Nell came back the next Saturday anyway."
- The title card changes to "Pencil me in."

**B. FAIR COPY (default)**

Requirements: any state that meets neither A nor C, including choosing "Finish it alone".

What happens:
- Nell completes the book by herself. It is beautiful and a little too neat.
- Dad carries it into the home while she waits in the car.
- He comes back and says, "She held it all afternoon. Wouldn't let the nurse take it." Nell answers, "...Next time."
- Final shot: a care-home window, with a hand waving at nobody in particular.
- The door is left open. The save file gains a note: "Visiting hours: Sat 2-4."

**C. CLEAN SHEET**

Requirements: choose "Let the Tidy finish", or Scribble Out 3 or more bosses. In the second case the other options are rubbed off the menu.

What happens:
- The book is blank and the house is sold.
- Months later, bored in class, Nell shades a pencil sideways across a blank page of the book. The grooves rise up white: a blot with a face, and the words "for Nell, so I don't lose you".
- She presses the eraser to it. Nothing happens, because you cannot rub out a groove.
- She asks Dad what day visiting hours are. The ending is sad, but it does not close the door.

**Replay hooks**
- There are 15 packable objects and only 6 Keep slots, so each run unlocks a different set of Underdrawing memories.
- New Game+ is called "Second Printing". It adds Oma's handwritten margin notes to every map and carries over the Endpapers gallery.
- Seeing all 15 memories across saves puts Blot on the title logo, dangling her legs.
signature_images: **CG1, the biscuit.** Oma sits at a kitchen table among packing boxes, holding out a dented biscuit tin with a warm stranger's smile. A finger-drawn doodle of a small blot shows in spilled sugar. Nell stands in the doorway in her oversized yellow raincoat.
**CG2, the open book.** The left page is a bright crayon town of teapot houses. The right page is rubbed grey with ghost lines still visible. Pink eraser crumbs crawl across the gutter like ants.
**CG3, Blot on the caption line.** She sits on a line of handwritten text and swings her legs. The words beside her are smeared away, leaving only "...my best m".

**CG4, the Clock That Can't.** A giant spool-tower clock looms over Button Square with the numbers 1-12 all crowded between 12 and 3. Tiny townsfolk stare up and a teaspoon councillor checks his wrist.
**CG5, the Staircase.** Enormous wooden steps climb into the clouds. On the wall are pencil height marks: "Nell 4, Nell 5 ... Nell 9". Above that is bare wood.

**CG6, the Stranger-in-the-Hall.** A cosy hallway has rose wallpaper and a coat stand. In it stands a towering coat-and-hat shape scribbled in black crayon so hard the paper has torn. A small raincoat-shaped silhouette is just visible inside the scribble.

**CG7, the attic.** Hundreds of unsent envelopes are pegged on washing lines like bunting in the attic dusk. Each bears a little drawing of a girl. The drawings get simpler from left to right until the last is only a smiling blot.
**CG8, holding on.** Nell grips Blot's hand as Blot's arm thins to a dotted line. Greyness spreads from the corners. Tuppence's cape and Oddment's ear are already half ghost-line.
**CG9, the Tidy unmasked.** A spotless white paper-cutout child lifts off its pink eraser cap. Underneath is Nell's own face, drawn very neatly, with no mouth. It holds a dustpan full of colors.

**CG10, two hands on one pencil.** An old spotted hand and a small smudged hand draw a yellow lamplight on the last page. Blot laughs in the corner.

**Ending C variant.** A page shaded in side-on graphite, with white grooves reading "for Nell, so I don't lose you".
enemy_concepts: **Dust Bunny.** A grey lint rabbit that sneezes itself apart. Missing Piece: a burrow. Missing Color: Green.
**Odd Sock.** A lone striped sock that hops and stomps while calling for its pair. Missing Piece: draw its twin. Missing Color: Blue.
**Button-Eye.** A loose coat button that scuttles on thread legs and stares unblinking. Missing Piece: its other eye. Missing Color: Yellow.
**Teacup Tempest.** A chipped teacup with a real thunderstorm inside. It pushes Red strokes. Missing Piece: a saucer to settle on.
**Eyeless Duck.** A rubber duck with a perfectly smooth face. It squeaks polite questions and is cute until it turns toward you.
**Sponge Nobody.** It absorbs the newest Swatch stroke every turn and swells. Wringing it out releases all the absorbed colors at once.
**Hairpin Heron.** An elegant bird bent from hairpins that pecks and leaves a fine clatter of pins. Its Heart Color is Violet.
**Half-Dog.** A shaky late drawing with six legs and two tails. It is delighted to see you and does not know it is "wrong". Finish it by naming it "Good Dog" and correcting nothing.
**Frame-Face.** A walking picture frame with a smudged portrait. It repeats the last skill a party member used.
**Step Creak.** A stair tread with a groaning mouth. It reads out your weight and age incorrectly.
**Mothball Choir.** Three moths singing slightly flat. Their song eats buffs. Missing Piece: a conductor's baton.
**Unsent Envelope.** A sealed letter that flutters and gives paper cuts. Missing Piece: an address. Nell writes her own.
**Ghost Line.** The faint groove of an erased townsperson. It is invisible until the Swatch holds a color. Finishing it restores that NPC to town.
**Crumbs.** A swarm of pink eraser crumbs that places Blank strokes. It cannot be Finished, only swept.
**Tidy-Up.** A small white paper helper with a dustpan. "Pardon me, you've got a bit of feeling just there." It removes your newest stroke.

**BOSSES**
- The Clock That Can't. Heart Color: Violet. Missing Color: Green. To Finish it, draw its numbers back.
- The Drain. Heart Color: Blue. To Finish it, Name three swallowed words.
- The Stranger-in-the-Hall. Heart Color: Deep Red. Missing Color: Blue. It is a terrified drawing of Nell. To Finish it, keep the page Blue while it rages.
- The Tidy. It uses the Blank Page and has no Heart Color until phase 2. After that, its Heart Color is whatever Nell's is.
pitch:imagery-first.exploration_and_puzzles:
**Exploration**
- Encounters are visible on the map as wobbling doodles, so they can be avoided.
- Save points are Oma's reading glasses: "You look through them. Everything is slightly too big. Saved."
- The main exploration tool is the Graphite Stick. Shading rubbed-out patches reveals ghost grooves: hidden bridges, erased signs and doorways into the Underdrawing.
- The daily packing choice visibly changes that night's maps, because a thrown-out object's prop is erased.
- Keepsakes are accessories, up to 6, each with a memory caption. Examples: the Biscuit Tin gives +20% item healing, and the Checked Tea-Towel lets Tuppence taunt for free.
- There are about 20 items, including Biscuit (30 HP), Cold Tea (Lead +3), Jam Spoon (revive), Pencil Shaving (cures Smear) and Correction Fluid (removes one Blank).

**Puzzles**
1. Button sorting logic in Button Square: two-hole and four-hole buttons, color, and coat clues.
2. Bathtub water levels with hot and cold taps and the plug, to float the ferry to three docks.
3. Staircase portrait-naming, using rubbings taken in the Underdrawing.
4. Ordering the attic letters by handwriting decay.
5. The Margin's perspective-line maze, where the only walkable ground is lines converging on the vanishing point.
6. Frottage riddles found throughout the world: shade a blank sign to read it.
pitch:imagery-first.antagonistic_force:
**The Tidy** is a child-sized figure cut from spotless white paper, with Nell's exact height and silhouette.
- It wears a pink rubber eraser cap and carries a dustpan and brush.
- It leaves no footprints and makes no sound except a soft rubbing noise.
- It is unfailingly polite and soothing. It leaves little thank-you notes ("Pardon the mess. Nearly done.") and genuinely believes it is helping: "There. Doesn't that hurt less?"
- It commands the Crumbs and the Tidy-Ups.

It is not the illness and it is not evil. It is Nell's own wish to forget Oma first, so that being forgotten cannot hurt. It cannot be destroyed. In the best ending Nell draws it a mouth, and it says the thing she could not: "I miss her and she's still here."
pitch:imagery-first.humor_and_charm:
**Running jokes**
- Sir Tuppence narrates himself in the third person and keeps getting stuck in crockery.
- The cutlery town council can never pass a motion. The fork abstains, the knife is "too divisive", and the teaspoon keeps stirring things up.
- Mx. Best-Offer, the shopkeeper, is a price tag on a string who will accept "2p, or best offer, or a sincere compliment".
- Coil the tape-measure snake lies about his length.
- Half-Dog follows you across maps whether or not you fought him.
- Oddment apologises to enemies and consoles chairs.
- Blot makes relentless stain puns.
- The Tidy's prim little notes start out funny and stop being funny.
- Each layer has one secret bench where the party just sits, and every character gets one unprompted line.

**In the real world**
- Dad's terrible packing-tape technique.
- Oma's third biscuit offer, which the player can accept all three times. Accepting all three earns the Keepsake "Three Biscuits".
pitch:imagery-first.music_direction:
**Leitmotif, "Oma's Hum"**

Seven notes in C major: G4 E4 A4 G4 C5 D4 E4. The phrase rises and falls, then ends unresolved on the third. It lands on the tonic C only in Ending A.

**Lo-fi treatment**

Tape wobble, a gentle low-pass filter and paper-rustle noise. The Tidy's music is deliberately dry and clean, which makes it unsettling.

**Tracks**
1. "Marram Lane". Nylon guitar, felt piano and a choir-pad hum of the motif.
2. "Thimble Hill" (title and town). Music box, ukulele-like plucks and glockenspiel at 96 bpm.
3. "Quilt Fields". Celesta, pizzicato strings and brushed kit.
4. "Pencil Fight!" (battle). Square lead playing the inverted motif, with bouncy bass, at 150 bpm. It has optional stems: strings enter in Blue moods, overdriven toms in Red and glockenspiel in Yellow.
5. "Bathtub Harbor". A vibraphone waltz with drip percussion.
6. "What Time Is It?" (boss). A 7/8 woodblock tick, detuned piano, and the motif with its notes crowded into one bar.
7. "One Step a Year". An ascending piano ostinato that gains one string voice per floor.
8. "Who Let You In" (boss). Saw lead, the motif in a minor key played too fast, and pounding toms.
9. "Unsent". A solo music box, slowed and pitch-dropped, with crackle.
10. "Pardon the Mess" (the Tidy). Prim harpsichord and celesta with no reverb. Whole bars drop to silence as if erased.
11. "Underdrawing". Choir pad and reversed piano, sparse.
12. "Clean Sheet" (final boss). It starts near-silent and the instruments return as colors return to the Swatch.
13. "The Last Page" (ending). Piano, nylon guitar and hum, with the motif resolved.
14. "Biscuit?". An 8-second comic jingle with a tuba-style bass and a kazoo-like synth.

**Sound effects (about 25)**

Pencil scratch for the cursor, crayon scribble hits in three timbres by color, an eraser rub, a page-peel transition, a lead-snap, a glasses-clink save, a Sign-flourish, a teacup clink, a paper tear for crits, and Blot's splat footsteps.
pitch:imagery-first.originality_notes:
**vs OMORI**
- There is no dream refuge hiding a death, no shut-in and no photo album. The secret is a living grandmother and a child's lie of avoidance.
- Feelings are not personal statuses in a rock-paper-scissors triangle. They are a shared three-slot color-mixing field that changes the rules for both sides, and erasure is a fourth force.
- Battles use a sketchbook-spread layout with a ground-line party row, not corner portraits.
- The skill resource is Lead.

**vs Undertale**
- There is no underground, no monster-versus-human conflict, no bullet-dodging and no meta-save plot.
- Non-violence is literal drawing completion, with a Sketch meter, Missing Piece and Missing Color.
- "Finishing is not fixing" is a theme of its own.
- There is no kill-count morality route. Endings hinge on four memory bosses, one hand-hold and a final choice.

**vs End Roll**
- The world is not a punishment or a trial and there is no drug-induced dream.
- The protagonist has harmed no one bodily. The guilt is an ordinary, forgivable childhood lie.
- The world is a gift made out of love.

**vs Ib**
- There is no gallery and no hostile artworks, no roses used as life, and no painted rival.
- The art is a family picture book. Its danger is erasure from within, caused by the reader herself.
- A real-world packing layer reshapes the drawn world.

**vs Re:Kinder**
- There is no town massacre or pact plot and no gore-cute shock.
- The unease comes from politeness, blankness and a wrongly drawn clock.

**Medium-native ideas of its own**
- Frottage exploration: shading a blank area to reveal grooves.
- Ghost-line party slots.
- A clock-drawing-test boss, handled with care.
- Illness is never the villain.

scores.strengths:
This is the freshest and most honestly scaled wound of the three. The secret is a small, survivable cruelty: Nell laughs along at her best friend, disowns him at the coat pegs, and leaves without a goodbye. It avoids the dead or dying relative entirely. Almost every player has done something like it, so the guilt reads as the player's own and not as borrowed tragedy.

The letters are the strongest writing in any pitch. The reveal inverts what Nell feared, because the letters are kind and not angry. Letter 1 apologises to her. Letter 8 is signed 'Tobias' where the others said 'Bix'. Letter 9 reads 'You were my best friend the whole time. Even that day.' None of this is melodrama, and it hurts because everyone behaves decently.

The real Tobias never appears and his forgiveness is never promised. That keeps the theme intact: an apology is something you send without knowing whether it will be answered.

The three endings are graded by emotional maturity, not by kill count:
- **Ending B:** the four-page letter that is 'mostly explanations of why it wasn't really her fault' is an unusually sharp observation about how children and adults really apologise.
- **Ending C:** the true letter physically cannot fit excuses.
- **Ending A:** the unwinnable final fight ends with being tucked in and told 'Some letters wait'. That is a humane way to do a bad ending.

The systems carry the theme:
- 'Never mind' is always the easiest menu option and is quietly counted.
- Story Lumps literally choke Nell.
- Nobody can clear their own Lump, so a friend has to Listen.
- Mister Nevermind is thanked and outgrown, not killed. He kept the ninth letter safest, and holding the umbrella over her while she reads is a sincere image.

Bix's self-awareness ('I'm not him. He's better than me. He gets hurt') turns the figment-friend device into an act of generosity and not a twist.

The humor is warm and character-based: pigeon bureaucracy, Mags's complaints, Kevin the pothole, Gerald with one hit point. It thins out on purpose as the Margin approaches.

Nothing here needs a content warning, and it still bites.
scores.weaknesses:
- **Closeness to OMORI.** An idealised dream friend invented to avoid guilt is the closest structural neighbour to OMORI among the three pitches. The differences are real: nobody dies, Bix knows what he is, and he leaves by choice. The build still has to foreground his self-awareness early so it does not read as a 'your friends aren't real' reveal.
- **The final postcard.** 'Dear Nell -' with a doodled gull partly takes back the promise that forgiveness is never guaranteed. It risks rewarding the apology with absolution after all.
- **The Stage scene.** All three options say 'laugh' and the game waits. It forces complicity and could feel coercive instead of confessional. It needs a light touch, and the CG6 'one bubble from the viewer's own position' device must not be over-egged.
- **Emotional distance in the party.** Mags and Noll are dream letters with real-world echoes. The real Magda and Ollie, who carry the healing, get thin screen time, so the final 'three kids at the pothole' may be under-earned.
- **A weak temptation.** Every incentive points toward opening the letters, because doing so removes Story Lumps. Avoidance never truly tempts the player, and Ending A is reached mainly by deliberate sabotage.
- **Heavy-handed risks.** The Laugh, as a floating HA HA, could tip into the obvious.
- **Small stakes.** Some players will find the stakes low unless Bix really is lovable within five minutes. That is a heavy load for the prologue writing.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
This pitch is my winner. Keep these and tighten them:
- The kind-not-angry letter sequence, with the Bix to Tobias signature shift.
- Endings graded by the honesty of the apology.
- 'Never mind' as the counted, easiest option.
- Story Lumps, plus Lumps that only a friend can clear.
- The antagonist who is thanked and hands over the last letter.
- The leitmotif that refuses to resolve, played with three-note chords only.

Recommended fixes:
- Make the final postcard more ambiguous, or cut away even earlier.
- Give opening each letter a felt cost, such as a dread beat or Nell hesitating. This makes not opening a real temptation.
- Expand Magda's and Ollie's daytime scenes.

scores.strengths:
This pitch has the best real-friend ensemble. Odo and Lin are physically present children, and their own unsaid things are small and true: the chip shop closing, and a parentified girl who has never said 'I need help'. Their arcs resolve in concrete real-world ways.

The car-park scene is the best 'friends stay' beat in any pitch. Wren Freezes, and the player has to control her friends and hand her glass one at a time. 'Nobody leaves.'

Other strengths:
- Pop's house labelled in shaky capitals (WREN'S CHAIR) and 'asked kindly who the little girl was' are observed with real tenderness.
- The Coat Pocket menu entry moves from 'Nothing I want to look at' to 'Not yet. But soon' to 'A letter. Read often'. It is a quiet, excellent plant.
- Ending B says outright that not-yet is allowed, which is humane.
- Ending C's tin can rattling 'Wren? You awake? Over.' means even the saddest ending leaves a friend on the line.
- Auntie Mum's 'It will never hurt. It will never anything.' is a chilling, sincere line.
- Tiny silly Pass confessions ('I do not actually like tea') make the heavy ones land.
- Odo's radio-procedure voice is instantly lovable.
scores.weaknesses:
- **Conventional core.** A beloved grandparent with dementia has died, there is guilt over not visiting, and an unread letter waits. Indie emotional games already cover this ground heavily.
- **Pre-packaged absolution.** A dementia patient, in one lucid afternoon, writes exactly the forgiveness Wren needs: 'You do not have to come and watch me go out.' Wren's apology therefore costs her less than Nell's does in pitch 0. Catharsis is handed to her from beyond the grave instead of being chosen under uncertainty.
- **Mascot sacrifice.** Pim ceasing to exist when opened is a familiar tearjerker lever. It is effective, but it is engineered.
- **Low hidden-truth payoff.** The prologue shows Pop, the coat and the labels, so only 'she stayed away' is concealed. Most players will guess it by Chapter 1.
- **Overstuffed for 80 minutes.** Pop, Odo's move, Lin's exhaustion, a whole town going silent and Auntie Mum all compete for time. The town-silence stakes dilute the personal story.
- **Hard mode inverts the theme.** Kept choices spawn harder optional enemies with extra loot, which makes avoidance the rewarding, completionist path.
- **A tidy epilogue.** 'Lin's mum takes a day shift' is too neat a fix.
- **Name confusion.** Auntie Mum's pun name blurs with Wren's actual mum.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
- **Reverse the Stage scene's controls.** Adapt the Freeze Up set-piece for pitch 0's Stage and coat-pegs sequence. Nell becomes Choked, and the player controls Bix, Mags and Noll, who must LISTEN to her one at a time. Nobody leaves.
- **Real-world friend scenes.** Give the real Magda and Ollie small, true unsaid things and a 'Say it / Keep it' beat each, so the epilogue friendship is earned.
- **Evolving menu text.** Change one menu line as the story moves, for example the Shoebox key item's description.
- **Explicit permission.** The middle ending should say that not-yet is allowed. Let a cleared save return to the final choice.
- **Tiny confessions.** Show one-line confessions when tokens are passed or Listened to, mostly silly ones so the rare heavy one lands.
- **A friend's voice in the sad ending.** Give Ending A a friend on the line in the final beat, as in the tin-can call.
- **Town details.** The compliment vending machine that, once fixed, only says 'You're doing fine.' Second-Class Stan the snail.

scores.strengths:
This pitch has the highest emotional peaks and the most truthful writing about dementia. 'She forgot again by teatime. Nell came back the next Saturday anyway' is the single best line across all three. It refuses the miracle-recognition cliche and makes love mean showing up.

The grandmother is alive, so the endings turn on an actionable choice and not on posthumous absolution.

The antagonist's insight is original and psychologically exact: the Tidy is Nell's wish to 'forget her first, before she finishes forgetting me'. It has no mouth. In the best ending Nell draws it one, and it says 'I miss her and she's still here'. That names anticipatory grief precisely.

Strong moments:
- The midpoint reveal that the Stranger-in-the-Hall is Oma's frightened drawing of Nell ('...Oh. That's you.') is a real gut-punch. It recontextualises and does not merely shock.
- 'Finishing is not fixing' and Half-Dog, named Good Dog with nothing corrected, embody good dementia-care ethics inside a joke.
- The 6-of-15 Keep packing choice makes the player the eraser, without scolding.
- Ending C's groove that cannot be rubbed out is native to the medium, sad, and still leaves the door open.
- The mandatory 'I lied.' selection is a sincere confession beat.
- Blot, 'my best mistake', is terrified of being corrected. She is the most lovable single character in any pitch.
- Tuppence's Stand In Front becoming Stand Beside is a lovely quiet arc.
scores.weaknesses:
- **Emotional overcrowding.** Eighty minutes must hold a dementia grandmother, a child's lie, a dead tailor grandfather as a sock rabbit, an exhausted father as a thimble knight, a fading ink child, young Oma as a guest, and unsent weekly letters. It risks stacking tearjerkers and tipping into melodrama.
- **Engineered fade scene.** Blot's hand-hold, with her survival gated on 12 or more Finished drawings, punishes the player by grading whether they 'loved enough'. That can feel manipulative instead of true.
- **Clinical material as a boss.** The Clock That Can't is a real diagnostic tool turned into a cute-creepy fight. The Drain swallows 'the word for kettle'. Both are striking but risky, because the player fights and can Scribble Out Oma's failing memories. Players with a relative in care may find this too raw or exploitative unless it is handled perfectly.
- **The Stranger reveal.** It frames the child as the monster in her grandmother's eyes, which needs careful aftercare.
- **A solitary story.** Nell has no peers. Every companion is a drawing of a family member, so the game has less friendship warmth than the tradition promises.
- **Familiar premise.** The dementia-grandparent starting point is well-worn even though this angle is new. A child falling into a relative's artwork brushes Ib's territory.
- **Mechanical gating.** Ending A requires 3 of 4 bosses Finished, Blot saved, and a greyed-out option. This sits awkwardly on top of something as delicate as a care-home visit.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
- **'Finishing is not fixing'.** Include at least one enemy or NPC whose Delivery requires correcting nothing, in the Half-Dog spirit.
- **Give the avoidance figure a voice.** Let Mister Nevermind's last line be the true sentence Nell could not say, as the Tidy's is.
- **The groove that cannot be erased.** In pitch 0's saddest ending and in the Margin, shading pencil over erased or VOID-stamped paper could reveal the grooves of Bix's handwriting and Nell's crossed-out drafts. Frottage could also be the Margin's exploration verb.
- **Day choices reshape the night.** Daytime choices visibly change that night's maps.
- **Dry epilogue captions.** Use unsentimental lines in the register of 'She forgot again by teatime...' in place of swelling prose.
- **Empty party slot.** After a goodbye, leave a dotted-outline slot that takes silent turns. For pitch 0, use it in a New Game+ or post-Bix moment.
- **Secret benches.** On a hidden bench the party just sits and each member says one unprompted line.
- **Comedy that also hurts.** The biscuit offered three times.
- **Mood-reactive battle music.** Optional stems that follow the dominant feeling on screen.
- **Endpapers-style credits.** A gallery of everyone you helped.

judge:emotional-resonance.verdict:
I pick pitch 0, LOST LETTER CLUB, as the winner on emotional resonance (scores: pitch 0 at 9, pitch 2 at 8.5, pitch 1 at 7.5).

**Why pitch 0 wins.** It is the only pitch whose hidden truth is not a dying or dead grandparent. It is an ordinary, survivable cruelty between children: laughing along, then hiding. Most players have committed it or suffered it.

- The scale suits an 11-year-old, and the pitch never reaches for shock. It still lands hard, because everyone in it behaves kindly. The letters Nell dreads turn out gentle, and the shift from 'Bix' to 'Tobias' does more than any death scene would.
- The three endings measure how honest the apology is. They range from avoidance, to a self-excusing four pages, to a short letter that cannot fit excuses. That is rarer and more adult than 'spared vs killed'.
- The systems say the same thing the story does. 'Never mind' is always the easiest option. Nobody can clear their own Lump. The final boss is thanked.

**Pitch 2, PENCIL ME IN, is a close second.** It has the highest individual peaks: 'forgot again by teatime... came back anyway', the mouthless Tidy, the groove that cannot be erased, and Half-Dog. It loses for three reasons:
- It is overcrowded with tearjerkers.
- It gates Blot's survival on the player's count of Finished drawings.
- It builds bosses out of clinical dementia imagery.

Those choices carry more risk of melodrama and of hurting players who are close to the subject.

**Pitch 1, Low Tide Letters, is third.** It has the best real-friend ensemble and the best 'nobody leaves' scene. Its core is the most conventional, though, and its posthumous letter hands Wren absolution instead of making her act without a promise.

**Grafts onto the winner**

From pitch 1:
- Make the real Magda and Ollie fuller, with their own small unsaid things.
- In the Stage sequence, reverse the controls so the player's friends must Listen to a Choked Nell.
- Change one line of menu text as the story moves.
- State outright that not-yet is allowed.

From pitch 2:
- Carry over 'Finishing is not fixing'.
- Put the pencil-groove reveal in the Margin and in the sad ending.
- Let Mister Nevermind say the true sentence at the end.
- Write the epilogue captions dry.

**Guard rails for the build**
- Establish Bix's self-awareness early, so the dream-friend device stays clearly distinct from OMORI.
- Keep the final postcard truly ambiguous, so forgiveness is never promised.
- Give opening each letter a felt cost, so avoidance is a real temptation.

scores.strengths:
The Heart Tray is fully specified with numbers: 5 slots, 4 token kinds, HOLD passives, six SAY effects, SWALLOW and LISTEN. It is structurally unlike an emotion triangle. Three things work especially well:
- **Lumps persist after battle.** Only a friend's LISTEN or a bench clears them. That gives exploration a real attrition loop, so benches and save points matter mechanically, and it expresses the theme through the system.
- **Story Lumps** tie real-world dialogue choices to combat for the cost of one counter. Bix being unable to hold Sore (it lands on Nell as a Lump) is cheap to build and tells story through play.
- **DELIVER blends with fighting.** Combat generates the tokens that addresses need, XP is equal on both routes, and scraps trade off against stamps. That is one balance curve to tune, not two. Wrong guesses feed the enemy tray toward a telegraphed Blurt, which creates readable tension.

The ending conditions are concrete and easy to track: a count of letters opened plus the Nevermind order and who Says each slot. The battle layout, a lined-paper sheet above a bottom row of stamp cards with perforated trays, is simple to draw on a 768x576 canvas. Thirteen maps are all describable as ground plus props. The Stage beat where the game waits for input costs almost nothing to build. The enemy gimmicks (Wrong Number, Blank Card, Inkblot, Eraser Mite, The Laugh) are all expressible in the token system without new subsystems.
scores.weaknesses:
**Token generation can stall DELIVER.** Tokens come mostly from reactive, unreliable triggers. Cross needs a miss, a block or being targeted twice. Scared needs a telegraphed Blurt or dropping below 30% Heart. Glad needs a finishing blow or a heal. Addresses are ordered and want a specific feeling at a specific time, so the player can end up waiting to be hurt in the right way. Nevermind's address opens with Scared, which means you have to be in danger on purpose. Only a few skills generate tokens deliberately.

**Teaching load is heavy for a 60-90 minute game.** The player has to learn 4 HOLD passives, 6 SAY outcomes that depend on the target, Brimming overflow, Lumps and Choked, enemy trays, Blurts and ordered addresses.

**Story Lumps can permanently cripple the protagonist.** Three "never mind" choices with no letters opened leaves Nell Choked with no SAY. That is thematically right, but it makes roughly the back half of the game less fun for exactly the players who most need engaging. Bix's Sore redirect can choke her faster still.

**Technical risks:**
- The nine-step per-colour recolour of Gullhaven needs hue-mask compositing, or up to 9 asset variants.
- The Stampwood fold-maze, which folds map corners to reconnect paths, is the hardest puzzle to build across all three pitches.
- "The Margin enterable from the edge of any dream map" multiplies hidden-room content.

**Smaller issues:** Fifteen regular enemies plus five bosses is slightly over scope. The 32-stamp Album is ambiguous: with about 20 enemy types, it is unclear whether stamps are per delivery or per type. The exploration loop is less time-budgeted than Pitch 1's; there are no per-chapter minute counts and no statement on visible versus random encounters.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
- **Persistent clog.** A blocked or sealed pocket slot that survives battle, which only a friend's action or a save point clears. This gives rock pools and benches mechanical weight.
- **Story Lumps.** A Kept real-world choice puts a lasting blocked slot on the protagonist until the matching truth is faced. Cap it at 2 so it never fully chokes her.
- **Equal XP for Deliver and defeat**, with the split only in currency versus collection. This removes the dual-track balance problem.
- **Enemy trays with a telegraphed Blurt** that LISTEN can cancel. This gives Listen a defensive use.
- **An Album or bestiary that remembers revealed addresses**, so repeat encounters skip the Listen tax.
- **SWALLOW** as a panic guard with a long-term cost.
- **Boss world-state:** Delivered bosses move into the hub as NPCs with a hobby, and Torn bosses leave an empty chair.
- **Enemies to port:** Wrong Number (Deliver only by Listening), Blank Card (you define its address), and The Laugh (unhurtable; you outlast it or Listen to it).
- **The "game waits as long as you need" input beat.**
- **A final letter composed from collected phrase-stamps** that cannot fit excuses.
- **Colour returning to the real world**, done as 3-4 canvas-filter steps instead of 9.
- **Mags's collectible bench complaints**, and Gerald the one-HP boss with a full intro.

scores.strengths:
This is the best-engineered battle loop of the three. One resource, sea-glass, serves as skill cost, stat modifier, Deliver currency and Spill risk all at once. Every sink competes with the others, so each turn has a real question: what do I Pass, to whom, and do I spend on power or on being heard?

- **Generation is reliable.** The guaranteed +1 home colour per turn means no stalling, unlike Pitch 0. Off-colour skill costs (Rattle is Red+Blue, Beachcomb is Green, I Need Help is Tumbled Red) mean you need friends' glass to use your best tools. That makes Pass routing the actual puzzle, not a free bonus.
- **Tumbled glass is a clean payoff** that reads visually: it counts double, carries no penalty, is safe from Spill, and unlocks Out Loud skill versions.
- **Spill supplies threat.** Five of the same raw colour cause 2 turns of lost control, and Red makes the character hit allies. This gives enemies a non-damage attack vector: they can stuff your pockets.
- **Knots are a short deduction puzzle.** Two or three slots resolve in 1-2 rounds. Mishearing costs something. Damage shakes loose the last filled slot, so the player has to commit to a route.
- **The mechanics carry the story.** The scripted Freeze Up, where you control the friends and must Pass to Wren, and the undamageable Empty Chair with a 7-slot Knot fed by all three friends, both need zero new systems.

The exploration loop is the only one with a time budget. Day is 5-8 minutes with three Say/Keep choices and a shop. Night is 15-20 minutes with visible roaming enemies, one puzzle, rock-pool saves with Skim, a shortcut and a boss. Chapters sum to about 84 minutes. Both outcomes of Say/Keep are rewarded: a Said choice gives a permanent starting Tumbled glass, and a Kept choice spawns an optional named fight with a Keepsake. That is a real replay hook.

Eleven maps are all ground plus props. All six puzzles are known implementable types: sort-by-colour (which doubles as a tutorial for the Knot language), pipe rotation, clocks, a memory relabel, a sokoban string line, and a colour sequence. Side effects are cheap: townsfolk dialogue decaying to "...", and the town track thinning each day by muting MIDI channels.
scores.weaknesses:
**Subsystem bloat is the main risk.** The pitch has Bond per pair, 6 Duets, a bespoke Out Loud rider on each of 26 skills, a 6th slot, 12 charms, Keepsakes, Grit levels, Stamps, Skim and 16 album letters. That is too many progression layers for 60-90 minutes and one engine. It must be trimmed:
- Reduce Duets to 3.
- Make Out Loud riders generic.
- Merge charms with Keepsakes.

**Dual-track growth is a balance trap.** Grit comes only from Hushing and Bond only from Delivering. A pure Deliverer never gains Heart, yet Ending A requires surviving three Delivered boss fights. Three player profiles would have to be tuned separately.

**Pass may be close to always correct, and it is slow.** It is a free action every turn for all 4 characters. That is up to 8 menu decisions per round on keyboard, and it needs a one-key fast path or battles will drag.

**Art budget pressure:**
- Up to 9 named optional Unsents spawned by Kept choices will break the ~80-image budget unless they reuse recoloured enemy art.
- The battle layout needs full-body battle sprites on top of the map sprites.
- Fifteen regular enemies plus five bosses is slightly over scope.

**Ending C's trigger reintroduces a kill-counter.** "Hush at least 60% of encounters" edges toward Undertale's structure and is unnecessary, because Auntie Mum's explicit offer already exists.

**The Empty Chair never attacks.** It needs its Blue-flood clock tuned carefully or the finale will have no tension.

**Misheard permanently destroying the glass, on top of a +25% enemy attack buff, may over-punish experimentation** in the early game.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
Winner. The core to keep:
- The Pass and Tumble confiding economy, with off-colour skill costs.
- Spill.
- Knots with personal boss slots that accept only Tumbled glass.
- The Say it / Keep it day loop feeding each night.
- The Day-then-Night time budget per chapter.
- The forced-Freeze-Up and Empty Chair set pieces.
- The sorting puzzle that teaches the colour language.
- Skim at save points.
- Town dialogue decaying to "...", and the town theme losing instruments each day.
- The Coat Pocket menu entry whose text changes by ending.

Trims to apply:
- 3 Duets (Wren plus each friend).
- 4 generic Out Loud riders.
- Charms merged with Keepsakes.
- Some Grit awarded on Delivery, or flat XP parity.
- Kept-spawned Unsents as recolours of existing art.
- The 60%-Hush ending trigger dropped.
- A single-key Pass shortcut.

scores.strengths:
The Swatch is the most structurally original idea of the three. A single shared 3-slot colour-mixing field changes the rules for both sides, and erasure (Blank strokes) acts as a fourth force. That is far from any per-character emotion status system. The mood table is fully enumerated, and the blends (Green, Orange, Violet, Muddle) are evocative.

- **The Graphite Stick frottage verb** is an excellent, cheap exploration tool. You interact with a rubbed patch to reveal a hidden bridge, sign or door, and the action itself carries the game's metaphor.
- **The packing choice** (15 objects, 6 Keep slots) is a strong replay hook. It visibly alters that night's maps through procedural erased patches.
- **Missing Piece bespoke actions and the Half-Dog "correct nothing" beat** give the non-violent route more charm per enemy than either other pitch.
- **Visible doodle encounters** and chapter minute-budgets summing to about 85 minutes are sound.
- **Twelve maps**, all describable as ground plus props.
- **Several puzzles are easy to build:** portrait matching, letter ordering, the perspective-line maze and frottage signs.
scores.weaknesses:
**The core mechanic is unbalanced as specified.**
- A 3-slot FIFO queue that takes a stroke from every coloured skill on both sides turns over completely within a single round when 4 allies and enemies are all pushing. Holding a mood for In Your Element is mostly luck and turn order.
- The default party is Blue Nell, Red Tuppence, Yellow Blot and Green Oddment. Played naturally, it drives the Swatch into Brown Muddle, where skills cost +1 Lead, accuracy drops 20% and Sketch gain is zero. The system punishes the player for using skills and pushes them toward colourless Jab and Outline turns.
- Many mood effects are symmetric, for example +20% dealt and +10% taken for everyone. They wash out unless Heart Colors differ.
- The stack of Pressure, Bold Line, Snap and Blend Flourish, added on top of Lead and Sharpen, brings complexity without a clear decision.

**Finishing is shallow.** Outline is free, colourless and worth +20. Four characters spamming it Finish a regular enemy in about 2 rounds, with no resource cost or deduction. That is a meter fill, not a puzzle. The Blot-survival threshold of "12 Finished drawings" is also ambiguous: it could mean unique types or a running count.

**Scope is the largest of the three:**
- Three art styles.
- Six playable sprite sets: Nell twice, Blot, Tuppence, Oddment and Dill.
- Ghost-line variants.
- Every one of about 15 Finished enemy types becomes a town NPC with a gift, which means extra map sprites and finished-state art. That breaks the ~80-image budget.
- Fifteen Underdrawing memory vignettes.
- A chase set-piece.
- A multi-state water-level puzzle.
- Handwriting-decay assets.
- Mood-synced music stems.

**Layout problem:** the side-by-side sketchbook battle layout leaves enemies only about 384px of width at 768x576.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
- **Graphite Stick frottage exploration.** Shade a rubbed or blank patch to reveal hidden paths, signs and secret rooms. Re-skinned for the winner, this could be rubbing sand or fog off half-buried labels in the Lull.
- **Missing Piece.** A one-time bespoke action per enemy that appears partway through a Delivery. "Helping is not fixing" is a rule worth keeping, as is the Half-Dog-style enemy where the right answer is to change nothing.
- **A scaled-down limited Keep box.** For example, 6 objects with 3 Keep slots, each doubling as an equippable Keepsake with a memory caption.
- **Ending options the player has not earned are drawn as greyed ghost lines** in the menu, not hidden.
- **The commit rule:** Deliver progress gets harder once an enemy is badly hurt.
- **Blank-style boss pressure.** A shared-field element only in the final boss fight: the boss fills a small shared strip with Blanks that the party clears by Passing. This gives one fight a different texture without building the whole Swatch.
- **A Sharpen-style guard** that also restores resource.
- **One secret bench per layer** where the party just sits and everyone gets a line.
- **An optional single reactive music stem** in the battle track.
- **Credits rolling over a gallery** of everything the player Delivered.
- **Save-point flavour text with a joke.**
- **The three-biscuits gag:** accept the same repeated offer every time and get a Keepsake.

judge:gameplay-feasibility.verdict:
Pitch 1, Low Tide Letters, wins on gameplay-feasibility. It was the only pitch where I could not find a structural flaw in the battle loop.

**Why Pitch 1 wins**
- Its battle system uses one resource, sea-glass, which serves as skill cost, stat modifier, Spill risk and Deliver currency at once. The +1 home colour per turn keeps generation reliable.
- Its off-colour skill costs make Pass, the act of confiding, the central tactical puzzle, not a free bonus.
- It is the only pitch with a time-budgeted exploration loop: Day choices feed Night content across 11 ground-plus-props maps, for about 84 minutes in total.
- All six puzzles are standard and implementable.
- The story climaxes run on the existing mechanics. The forced Freeze Up and the undamageable Empty Chair need no new systems.

**What Pitch 1 must change**
- Cut Duets to 3.
- Make the Out Loud riders generic.
- Merge charms into Keepsakes.
- Reuse recoloured art for the Unsents spawned by Kept choices.
- Fix the Grit-versus-Bond split by giving XP parity on Delivery.
- Drop the 60%-Hush ending trigger.
- Add a one-key Pass shortcut so rounds stay fast.

**Pitch 0, Lost Letter Club, is a strong second.** Its Lump-and-Listen interdependence, persistent Lumps and Story Lumps are the best link between exploration and battle in any of the pitches. Three problems hold it back:
- Tokens are generated reactively while addresses are ordered, so DELIVER can stall.
- Story Lumps can permanently choke the protagonist.
- The fold-maze and the nine-step recolour are real technical risks.

**Pitch 2, Pencil Me In, has the most original mechanic structure but is last on this lens.**
- The 3-slot FIFO Swatch turns over completely every round.
- The default party pushes itself into Muddle.
- Finishing by spamming free Outlines is shallow.
- Its content scope blows the 80-image budget: an NPC version of every enemy, 15 memory scenes, six sprite sets and three art styles.

**What to graft onto the winner**
- From Pitch 0: persistent blocked slots that only a friend or a save point clears; a capped Story-Lump link from Kept choices; an album that remembers Knots; Blurt telegraphs that Listen can cancel; Delivered bosses moving into the hub; and the Wrong Number, Blank Card and The Laugh enemy gimmicks.
- From Pitch 2: the frottage exploration verb; Missing Piece bespoke actions built on the "helping is not fixing" rule; ghost-line menu options for unearned endings; and a small limited Keep box.

scores.strengths:
The wound is the most original of the three. Nobody dies and nobody is ill. Nell was simply cruel to a friend who is alive and kind, and he never promises forgiveness. None of the five inspirations work at that small, ordinary scale.

Mechanically:
- Hold/Say/Swallow/Listen, with Lumps that only a friend can clear, is not an emotion triangle.
- The ordered-address DELIVER is fed by the same tokens that fighting generates, so it is not ACT-then-spare.
- Regular fights are not scolded.
- Endings depend on letters opened rather than a body count.

Several beats belong to the tradition without being lifted from it:
- The Stage, where every option says "laugh" in fainter pencil and the game waits.
- Story Lumps earned by real-world "never mind" choices.
- A final boss who is thanked and hands over what he kept safe.
- An apology composed from phrase-stamps that cannot fit excuses.
- Ending B admitting the apology is still partly about herself.
- The unionised pigeon civil service.

The bottom-row stamp cards avoid the four-corner layout.
scores.weaknesses:
Under the postal skin the skeleton matches OMORI almost beat for beat, and the pitch's originality notes do not admit it.

1. Nell invents a bright refuge, enters it at bedtime, and alternates it with a drained real world across three numbered days and nights.
2. The friend she wronged appears as an idealised figment who cannot remember the incident and glitches when he gets near it.
3. Mister Nevermind is an internal repression-guardian who voids anything approaching the truth. That is what Omori does to the dream world when Basil starts remembering.
4. The Margin is a blank white-paper layer beyond the bright world, with an unhurtable stalker (The Laugh). It reads as White Space/Black Space plus Something.
5. The truth is reassembled from nine collectible documents, like the photo album.
6. The trauma is a music performance and the true ending is the song finally played whole. That sits very close to the recital and duet.
7. Dream party members have real-world counterpart kids. This is OMORI's dual cast.
8. In the bad ending the repressor tucks her in.

It is also End Roll's skeleton: a guilt-dream populated by an unharmed version of the person you hurt.

The token set is OMORI's four emotions with the same colours.
- Sore (blue) gives +DEF and -SPD, which is the Sad profile exactly.
- Cross (red) gives +ATK and -DEF, which is the Angry profile exactly.
- Glad (yellow) gives crit, matching Happy's luck.
- Scared (violet) matches Afraid.
- Stacking intensity stands in for the three tiers.

The structure on top is new, but the brief said "not just renamed emotions".

Other echoes:
- The single-option forced prompts recall OMORI's forced-action moments.
- Delivered bosses moving into the hub recalls Undertale's epilogue.

Generic elements:
- A grey real world against a coloured dream.
- The mustard raincoat and red wellies, which all three pitches share.
- The leitmotif, which is note-for-note the same as pitch 1's.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
- **Real-world avoidance as a battle handicap.** The Story Lump idea: every avoidant real-world choice leaves a persistent handicap that only facing the truth removes. On the winner, a "fine" or a Throw-out could start fights with one Blank already in the Swatch until the matching Underdrawing memory is opened.
- **Only a friend can clear it.** "You cannot clear your own Lump, only a friend can." Apply this to Snapped lead or Blank removal.
- **The patient prompt.** The game waits as long as the player needs on the one hurtful option. Use it for the "I lied" moment.
- **A thanked antagonist.** The final antagonist is thanked and hands over something it kept safe.
- **Assembled final message.** The final letter or caption is built from phrases collected during play and is too short to hold excuses.
- **Honest middle ending.** Ending B shows a sincere but still self-centred first attempt.
- **Enemy designs:**
  - Blank Card becomes whatever you say to it.
  - Wrong Number can only be resolved by Listening three times.
  - Inkblot mirrors your own state.
  - Gerald has a full boss intro and 1 HP.
- **Humour:**
  - Mags files a collectible complaint about every save point ("Dear Game, I did not consent to being saved").
  - Redeemed bosses take up hobbies in the hub.
  - The vending machine is proud of selling only envelopes.
  - The deadpan prop inspections ("Its name is Kevin").

scores.strengths:
It breaks OMORI's cast structure decisively.
- The friends are real, physically present, and carry their own secrets.
- The otherworld is communal, a whole town's unsaid words. It is not the protagonist's private refuge.
- The secret is an absence (visits not made), not an act.

Pass/Tumble is the freshest way on the panel to make feelings the heart of combat.
- A feeling kept raw warps you and can Spill.
- The same feeling handed to a friend loses its penalty and counts double.
- Each hand-over shows a one-line confession.

The theme is built into the rules, and nothing in the five games resembles it. The emotion set (Fondness, Worry, Temper, Wonder) is also the least OMORI-coded of the three.

New hooks:
- Pim is a party member who is secretly the unread letter in your own menu ("Coat Pocket: Nothing I want to look at").
- Daytime Say it/Keep it choices spawn that night's named enemies.

The peaceful path is a real resource puzzle rather than ACT-then-spare.
- Say spends the same glass that powers skills.
- Damage shakes filled slots loose.

None of the five inspirations would produce these images:
- The Empty Chair in a fogged car park.
- Blank labels on every object in Ending C.

Ending B's "not-yet is allowed" and Ending C's tin-can way back are humane and distinctive. The tideline layout is clear of the four-corner design.
scores.weaknesses:
Undertale leaks in through the reward split.
- Hush gives Grit and Levels. Deliver gives no levels but friendship power. That is the LV-versus-bonds dichotomy.
- Ending C fires on "Hush all bosses and 60% of encounters". That is a kill-counter route, which the pitch's originality notes explicitly deny having.

Auntie Mum is a tall, gentle, maternal gatekeeper who sincerely wants to keep children safe forever and offers free heals during her own fight. With that name on top, the Toriel resonance is strong (and Coraline's Other Mother). Her wax-seal mouth and printed cards are her own.

Smaller echoes:
- Three day/night cycles plus a friend moving away recalls OMORI's countdown spine.
- The verb "Pass" collides with Kel's "Pass to..." follow-ups.
- Bond-unlocked pair Duets resemble OMORI's follow-up attacks.
- Raw Red is the Angry stat profile.
- Each friend's boss only yields when that friend says their hidden truth. That is Persona 4's shadow structure. It is outside the five, but well-worn.
- A final encounter that cannot be damaged is standard in this tradition.

The zones are stock surreal-RPG: an empty funfair, an infinite filing office, a lighthouse.

The identity is diffuse. Post, sea-glass, tin-can phones, rope knots and tides are several metaphor systems competing, so it has less of a single signature than the other two. The dementia-grandparent-plus-unread-letter premise is affecting but more conventional than it presents itself.

It shares the raincoat-and-wellies girl with the other two pitches and the identical leitmotif with pitch 0.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
- **Shared feelings are stronger.** The Pass/Tumble principle: a feeling handed over by a friend is stronger and loses its drawback. Rename "Pass" to avoid the OMORI collision. On the winner, a stroke pushed at an ally's request could count double or skip its Tint penalty.
- **One-line confessions.** Show them on every hand-over, mostly tiny and silly ("I do not actually like tea"), so the heavy ones land.
- **A changing menu entry.** Its description reads "Nothing I want to look at", then "Not yet. But soon.", then "A letter. Read often."
- **Daytime avoidance spawns night enemies.** Keeping something back by day creates a named optional enemy that night. It pairs naturally with the winner's packing loop: a thrown-out object returns as a named Ghost Line.
- **The Empty Chair.** A final encounter that does not attack, cannot be damaged, and is survivable only through allies' support.
- **Humane endings:**
  - Ending B's explicit "not-yet is allowed", with a reloadable final choice.
  - Ending C's last prompt as a way back into New Game+.
- **The letter's line.** "Being loved does not need a name on it." It fits the winner's theme exactly.
- **Small details:**
  - A two-line mini-story per redeemed enemy in the album.
  - The Four Clocks puzzle, solved by setting one deliberately wrong and taking the door marked LATE.
  - Whisper Tubes garble humour ("Weird muffin").
  - The compliment vending machine that, once fixed, says only "You're doing fine."
  - Wrong Label, the apologetic teacup labelled DOOR.

scores.strengths:
This is the only pitch whose otherworld is not the guilty protagonist's own refuge, which is the spine OMORI and End Roll share. Here it is someone else's act of love, authored by the person who is forgetting her. The bosses are Oma's hard memories, drawn by a failing hand. That inversion is new to the tradition.

Standout beats:
- The Stranger-in-the-Hall reveal, where the monster is you as seen through frightened eyes, is the most original single beat in any pitch.
- The Clock That Can't, a clock-drawing test as a boss, is startling and humane.

The ideas are native to the paper-and-pencil medium in a way none of the five manage:
- Frottage with the Graphite Stick reveals grooves.
- The Underdrawing is made of blue construction lines.
- Party slots can become ghost lines.
- Daytime Keep/Give/Throw packing (6 of 15 objects) rubs out that night's props.
- Ending C's "you cannot rub out a groove".

The Swatch is structurally the furthest of the three mechanics from OMORI.
- It is one shared three-slot first-in-first-out field that both sides paint.
- Moods come from colour mixing.
- Heart Colour makes every fight a tug-of-war.
- Blanks act as a fourth force.
- There is no per-character status and no advantage wheel.

Finishing differs from Undertale's route.
- It is driven by mood and a Sketch meter rather than a menu of acts.
- It pays 70% XP, so it avoids Undertale's zero-EXP morality.
- "Finishing is not fixing" (Half-Dog) is a thesis of its own.

Illness is never the villain. The sketchbook-spread layout is clearly not four corners. The pitch also makes the mandated crayon art style part of the fiction, so the whole package has one coherent signature.
scores.weaknesses:
There are two real flags, and the originality notes gloss over both.

**1. Ib adjacency.** A girl visiting with a parent is pulled into the living world of one artist's work.
- The enemies are hostile artworks, which the notes wrongly deny.
- The companions are drawings.
- The best ending is hard-gated on whether a companion survives, as Ib's endings are on Garry.
- The Landing of Framed Faces, plus the Frame-Face walking portrait, is the most Ib-coded content in any pitch.
- A crayon storybook zone recalls Ib's Sketchbook area.

**2. The Tidy.** It is a colourless, mouthless, neat child-double of the protagonist who wants painless blankness, fought as the final boss amid "Blank Page" and "Clean Sheet" imagery. It will read as Omori and White Space unless it is carefully differentiated.

Other flags:
- The Stranger as a towering black scribble sits close to OMORI's scribble-horror Something look.
- The Swatch primaries are Blue, Red and Yellow, with a Tint-to-Deep intensity ladder. Their stat directions mirror Sad (defensive, slower), Angry (hits harder, takes more) and Happy (faster). That is OMORI's exact colour code, even though the structure differs.
- Missing Piece bespoke actions are ACT-flavoured.
- A friendly dog pacified by kindness is Undertale's most recognisable joke.
- Finished enemies moving into the hub is like Undertale's epilogue.
- Ending C, triggered by "Scribble Out 3+ bosses" with options rubbed off the menu, is a body-count route lock with Undertale-style menu tampering.
- Party members as avatars of real family is OMORI's dual cast. It is mitigated because they are Oma's drawings, not Nell's fantasy.

Generic outside the five:
- A tiny world of lost household objects.
- Falling into a book.
- The raincoat-and-wellies girl, identical to the other two pitches.
scores.ideas_worth_grafting:
**Keep as the irreplaceable core**
- The world as Oma's gift, not Nell's refuge.
- The Stranger reveal.
- The Clock That Can't.
- Frottage and the Underdrawing.
- The packing loop.
- Ghost-line slots.
- Drawing the Tidy a mouth.
- The groove ending.

**Required originality fixes**
1. **De-Ib the staircase chapter.**
   - Replace the Landing of Framed Faces and the Frame-Face enemy with the height-mark wall, mantelpiece snapshots or a button tin of faces.
   - Use no gallery rooms and no pursuing portraits.
   - Do not make Blot's survival a hard Garry-style gate. Let it colour the endings instead of locking them.
2. **Differentiate the Tidy from Omori.**
   - Make it talkative, fussy and craft-paper physical (eraser cap, dustpan, notes).
   - Never give it a white-void hub or blank-stare monochrome-boy staging.
   - Keep the mouth-drawing resolution.
3. **Redraw the Stranger.** Make it Oma's frantic multi-colour overworked crayon on torn paper, not a black shadow figure.
4. **Re-map the Swatch.**
   - Blue, Red and Yellow should not mirror the Sad, Angry and Happy stat directions.
   - Drop the three-step naming.
   - Prefer rule changes over stat swings, and put the emphasis on the blends.
5. **Remove the body-count trigger and menu tampering from Ending C.** Drive it from the final choice and the packing decisions.
6. **Half-Dog's interaction must never be "pet".**
7. **Give Nell a silhouette that is not mustard raincoat plus red wellies.** Lean on the two-ended checking pencil, the graphite smudges and her left-handedness.

judge:originality.verdict:
**Pitch 2 (PENCIL ME IN) wins on originality at 8. Pitch 1 (Low Tide Letters) is a close second at 7.5, and pitch 0 (LOST LETTER CLUB) scores 5.5.**

**Why pitch 2 wins**

It is the only pitch that escapes the skeleton OMORI and End Roll share, where the otherworld is a guilty dreamer's private refuge. Its world is a gift made by the person who is forgetting the protagonist, and its bosses are that person's memories. Its central reveal is that the monster is you, seen through frightened eyes. None of the five games has a beat like that.

Its mechanics and exploration verbs come from its paper-and-pencil medium and owe nothing to the inspirations:
- The Swatch is a shared colour-mixing field.
- Finishing completes a drawing rather than sparing or killing it.
- Frottage reveals what was erased.
- The Underdrawing is a hidden layer of first sketches.
- Packing by day erases props by night.

It also turns the required crayon art style into part of the fiction, which gives it the most unified identity of the three.

**Fixes pitch 2 needs before production**

- **Ib adjacency.** Remove the framed-portrait landing and the walking-portrait enemy. Do not hard-gate the best ending on a companion's survival.
- **The Tidy.** Stage it so it cannot be read as a colourless Omori double in a white void.
- **The Stranger.** Draw it in frantic multi-colour crayon rather than as a black scribble silhouette.
- **The Swatch.** Re-map the primaries so Blue, Red and Yellow do not mirror OMORI's Sad, Angry and Happy colour code and stat directions.
- **Ending C.** Drop the body-count ending trigger and the menu-option tampering, both of which echo Undertale.
- **The protagonist's look.** Change the raincoat-and-wellies silhouette that all three pitches share.

**Why the others lose**

Pitch 1 has the best confiding mechanic (Pass/Tumble) and the single best character hook: Pim, the unread letter in your own pocket. It loses narrowly for four reasons:
- Its Hush-gives-levels, Deliver-gives-bonds split and its 60% Hush ending echo Undertale.
- Its maternal gatekeeper antagonist echoes Toriel.
- Its zones are generic.
- Its metaphors are diffuse.

Pitch 0 has the most original wound, an ordinary cruelty toward a friend who is alive. Structurally, though, it is a softened transposition of OMORI:
- A nightly self-made refuge.
- A figment friend who cannot remember.
- An internal repressor who voids the truth.
- A blank white layer with a stalker.
- Collectible truth documents.
- A music-performance trauma.

Its four tokens are also OMORI's four emotions with identical colours and stat profiles.

**Ideas to graft onto the winner**

From pitch 1:
- Feelings that get stronger when a friend hands them to you, with one-line confessions.
- The menu entry whose description changes.
- Avoided things returning as named enemies.
- The un-damageable, non-attacking final encounter.
- The "not-yet is allowed" ending.
- The line "Being loved does not need a name on it."

From pitch 0:
- Real-world avoidance leaving persistent battle handicaps.
- "Only a friend can clear it."
- The patient forced-confession prompt.
